claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially a high-temperature single-phase BCC alloy.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by the Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC phases.
Kinetic barriers, including sluggish diffusion, jointly govern phase stability and transformation extent in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
At high temperature, ΔG_BCC–FCC favors BCC stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
On cooling Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, ΔG_BCC–FCC shifts increasingly toward FCC stability.
A thermodynamically favored BCC-to-FCC transformation will occur only if kinetic barriers permit sufficient atomic rearrangement.
Slower cooling provides sufficient atomic mobility to produce a larger FCC fraction.
Rapid cooling preserves metastable BCC because there is insufficient time for diffusion.
Slow-cooled samples will contain more FCC at lower temperatures than rapidly cooled samples, which will largely retain BCC.
Measured phase fractions should correlate with calculated ΔG_BCC–FCC trends.
Slow cooling and rapid quenching will be compared while chemical composition is held constant.
The baseline is the as-annealed high-temperature BCC alloy subjected to a standard cooling process.
The hypothesis is limited to a thermal regime in which phase transformations are experimentally accessible.
The composition is assumed to remain fixed at Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during testing.
Ultra-rapid quenching or annealing far beyond the designed range may produce behavior outside the model.
The quantitative ΔG_BCC–FCC values and kinetic-barrier magnitudes are uncertain.
Failure to observe a significant FCC increase under slow cooling relative to rapid cooling would falsify the proposed thermodynamic–kinetic explanation.
